notes: Ruling slot 0 = Sekber Golkar. Coalition slot 13 holds Kopkamtib (security command as non-aligned authoritarian partner); ABRI itself stays in 22 per MD. NU in 1, PNI in 14 (popularity slot), Parmusi in 12, PKI in 4 per MD, Murba in 19. Bappenas technocrats ('Berkeley Mafia') as libertarians in 16, Pertamina as oligarchs in 15. Sukarnoist remnants in 6 (KKO loyalists) and 7 (Barisan Sukarno).

0.name: Sekretariat Bersama Golongan Karya
0.text:
The Joint Secretariat of Functional Groups was created by army officers in October 1964 to unite anti-communist unions, professional bodies and civil servants against the PKI. Under President Suharto's New Order it has become the regime's electoral vehicle, being reshaped by his political aides for the general election planned for 1971.

Golkar rejects ideological party politics in favour of Pancasila, stability and economic development, and promises order after the chaos of Guided Democracy. It backs Western aid, foreign investment and close ties with the United States and Japan. Its leverage lies in the army, the civil service and the state budget, which it uses to recruit voters.

1.name: Partai Nahdlatul Ulama
1.text:
Nahdlatul Ulama was founded in 1926 by Hasyim Asy'ari and Wahab Hasbullah as the association of traditionalist ulama and their pesantren, and has contested elections as a party since 1952. Led by Idham Chalid, it is the largest Islamic party and its youth wing Ansor took a leading part in the destruction of the PKI in 1965-66.

NU defends traditional Sunni practice, the authority of the kyai and the interests of rural Java's pious santri communities. It cooperates with the New Order while resisting Golkar's encroachment and military interference in its ranks. Its strength lies in East and Central Java, where millions follow their kyai's lead.

2.name: Kesatuan Aksi Mahasiswa Indonesia
2.text:
The Indonesian Students Action Front was formed in October 1965 by anti-communist student organizations and led the street protests of 1966 that helped bring down Sukarno. Its activists, the self-styled Generation of 1966, now include ministers' advisers and parliamentarians, while others have turned critic as corruption grows under the New Order.

KAMI's reform wing demands clean government, rule of law, press freedom and genuine elections rather than a military-managed vote. It favours a market economy and Western ties, but warns against generals and cronies enriching themselves. Its leverage lies in the campuses of Jakarta and Bandung and in a press that amplifies student protest.

3.name: Partai Sosialis Indonesia
3.text:
The Socialist Party of Indonesia was founded by Sutan Sjahrir in 1948 as a party of the democratic left and was banned by Sukarno in 1960. Sjahrir died in exile in 1966, and the New Order has refused to legalize the party, though its figures, such as Subadio Sastrosatomo, remain active and its economist Sumitro Djojohadikusumo serves as Minister of Trade.

The PSI stands for democratic socialism, parliamentary government, civil liberties and planned modernization with Western help. Its base is small, but its alumni hold influential posts among intellectuals, journalists, economists and officers, giving it an influence on policy far exceeding its electoral weight.

4.name: Partai Komunis Indonesia
4.text:
The Communist Party of Indonesia, founded in 1920 and once the largest communist party outside the socialist bloc, was destroyed after the 30 September Movement of 1965. Hundreds of thousands of members were killed or imprisoned, chairman Aidit was shot, and its South Blitar guerrilla base was crushed in 1968; a delegation under Jusuf Adjitorop survives in Beijing.

The outlawed party calls for the overthrow of Suharto's military regime through people's war, land reform and an end to dependence on imperialism. Underground cells persist among former members, while tens of thousands of political prisoners are held on Buru Island and in prison camps across the archipelago.

5.name: Pasukan Gerilya Rakyat Sarawak
5.text:
The Sarawak People's Guerrilla Force was formed from Chinese communist youth of Sarawak, trained and armed by Indonesia during the Confrontation with Malaysia. After 1966 the New Order turned against its former allies, and the guerrillas, with the allied Paraku, now fight the Indonesian army in the jungles of West Kalimantan.

They wage a Maoist people's war against the Indonesian and Malaysian governments, aiming at a communist North Kalimantan. Their base lies among rural Chinese communities, many forcibly uprooted by army-incited Dayak attacks in 1967. Though isolated and dwindling, they tie down troops and remain the last armed communist force in the archipelago.

6.name: Hitam Kata Bung Karno
6.english: Black If Bung Karno Says So
6.text:
Black If Bung Karno Says So takes its name from the famous oath of the Navy's Marine Corps, the KKO, that it would follow Sukarno to the end. Its commander, Lieutenant General Hartono, was removed in 1968 and sent abroad as an ambassador, but Sukarnoist sentiment survives among Marines, naval and air force officers and veterans of the revolution.

These officers reject the New Order's turn to Washington and foreign capital and long for the anti-imperialist, Nasakom era of Guided Democracy. They have no organization and are watched by army intelligence, yet their loyalty to the ailing ex-president and their weapons make them a latent threat to Suharto's control.

7.name: Barisan Sukarno
7.text:
The Sukarno Front was proclaimed in January 1966 by Sukarno's loyalists, with Foreign Minister Subandrio as its moving spirit, to defend the president against the army and the student movement. It was swiftly banned; Subandrio sits in prison, and Sukarno, stripped of power in 1967, lives under house arrest in Jakarta in failing health.

Its surviving adherents want Guided Democracy restored: strong presidential rule, the unity of nationalism, religion and communism, anti-imperialism and close ties with the non-aligned and socialist world. They draw on loyalist PNI members and officials, and Sukarno's name still commands deep affection among millions of ordinary Javanese.

8.name: Kerukunan Keluarga Tabot
8.text:
The Tabot Families of Bengkulu descend from the sepoys and craftsmen brought from India by the British in the eighteenth century, who introduced the Tabot festival commemorating the martyrdom of Imam Husayn in Muharram. The families still build the tabot towers and lead the processions each year, joined by the townspeople of Bengkulu and Pariaman.

Their tradition preserves a gentle Shia devotion woven into local Malay culture: mourning for the Prophet's family, communal solidarity and tolerance toward their Sunni neighbours. They seek no political power, but they guard the only living Shia ritual in the archipelago against reformist critics who denounce it as heresy.

9.name: Kaum Karbala
9.text:
The People of Karbala are a small circle of Hadhrami Arab-descended Indonesians in Bangil, Pekalongan and Jakarta who have studied Shia texts and corresponded with clerics in Najaf and Qom. Against the overwhelmingly Sunni environment of Indonesian Islam, they meet discreetly to mourn Imam Husayn and read the works of Shia scholars.

They hold that religious authority belongs to the qualified jurist and regard secular, Western-backed rulers as illegitimate. Their circle is tiny and viewed with hostility by both the government and Sunni ulama, but their contacts abroad bring revolutionary clerical ideas into the Arab-Indonesian community.

10.name: Persatuan Tarbiyah Islamiyah
10.text:
The Islamic Education Movement was founded in 1928 in West Sumatra by Sheikh Sulaiman ar-Rasuli to defend the traditional Shafi'i school and the surau against Islamic modernists. It became a political party after independence and, after leaning toward Sukarno in the early 1960s, now supports the New Order and prepares to contest the 1971 election.

Perti defends traditional Islamic learning, the authority of the ulama and respect for established government, preferring accommodation with the state to confrontation. Its base lies among the Minangkabau religious schools and their students in Sumatra, and it serves the regime as a loyal Islamic counterweight to Masyumi's heirs.

11.name: Darul Islam / Tentara Islam Indonesia
11.english: Darul Islam / Islamic Army of Indonesia
11.text:
Darul Islam proclaimed the Islamic State of Indonesia in West Java in 1949 under Sekarmadji Maridjan Kartosuwiryo and waged a long insurgency that spread to Aceh and South Sulawesi. Kartosuwiryo was captured and executed in 1962, and Kahar Muzakkar was killed in 1965, but veterans of the movement maintain clandestine networks.

The movement rejects Pancasila and the secular republic and seeks an Islamic state governed by sharia, by armed struggle if necessary. Its strength lies in West Java villages, the sons of former fighters and the memory of jihad, and army intelligence watches it closely while seeking to manipulate it.

12.name: Partai Muslimin Indonesia
12.text:
The Indonesian Muslims' Party was founded in 1968 as a vehicle for the modernist Muslims of the banned Masyumi, whose former leaders the government barred from its leadership. Chaired by Djarnawi Hadikusumo of Muhammadiyah after the regime vetoed Mohammad Roem's election, it is under constant pressure from the army's political operatives.

Parmusi stands for modernist Islam, Islamic values in public life, constitutional government and economic development with an entrepreneurial Muslim middle class. It draws on Muhammadiyah, urban traders and the Outer Islands, especially Sumatra, where Masyumi was once strongest, and hopes to rally the modernist vote in the coming election.

13.name: Komando Operasi Pemulihan Keamanan dan Ketertiban
13.english: Operational Command for the Restoration of Security and Order
13.native_full: Komando Operasi Pemulihan Keamanan dan Ketertiban
13.text:
The Operational Command for the Restoration of Security and Order was created by Suharto in October 1965 to crush the PKI and has become the New Order's extra-constitutional security apparatus, commanded since 1969 by General Maraden Panggabean. It can arrest, interrogate and detain without trial, and it screens officials, candidates and journalists.

Kopkamtib places order and stability above law, treating communism, Sukarnoism and radical Islam as permanent threats. Pragmatic rather than ideological, it serves whoever controls the presidency. Its leverage lies in its vast powers of surveillance and detention, which make it the indispensable partner of Golkar's rule.

14.name: Partai Nasional Indonesia
14.text:
The Indonesian National Party, rooted in Sukarno's nationalist party of 1927, was the largest party of the 1955 election. Purged of its left wing under army pressure in 1966, it is led since Osa Maliki's death in 1969 by Hadisubeno Sosrowerdojo, though many members still revere the ousted Sukarno.

The PNI espouses Marhaenism, Sukarno's populist nationalism for the small farmer, and secular, religiously tolerant government. Its base is in the Javanese civil service, the abangan villages of Central and East Java and Bali. The regime distrusts its Sukarnoist sympathies and works to pull its officials into Golkar before the election.

15.name: Perusahaan Tambang Minyak dan Gas Bumi Negara
15.native_full: Perusahaan Tambang Minyak dan Gas Bumi Negara
15.text:
Pertamina, the state oil company formed in 1968 from the merger of Permina and Pertamin, is run by General Ibnu Sutowo as a personal empire. It controls production-sharing contracts with foreign oil companies and spends its revenues on ventures from shipping and steel to hotels, largely outside the budget.

It embodies the New Order's fusion of generals and business: profits finance the army, political funds and the patronage networks of senior officers, while Chinese-Indonesian partners handle trade and finance. Its leaders favour foreign investment and minimal oversight, and their wealth gives them access to the palace and immense weight in economic policy.

16.name: Badan Perencanaan Pembangunan Nasional
16.text:
The National Development Planning Agency is chaired by Widjojo Nitisastro, head of the University of Indonesia economists known as the Berkeley Mafia, alongside Ali Wardhana, Emil Salim and Mohammad Sadli. They tamed hyperinflation after 1966 and launched the first Five-Year Development Plan in April 1969.

The technocrats favour balanced budgets, stable money, open doors to foreign investment and aid through the Inter-Governmental Group on Indonesia, and deregulation of trade. They oppose economic nationalism and wasteful spending by military enterprises. Their leverage lies in Suharto's trust and in the confidence of Western donors and the World Bank, which fund the plan.

17.name: Mahasiswa Pencinta Alam Universitas Indonesia
17.text:
The University of Indonesia Nature Lovers were founded in 1964 by students including Soe Hok Gie, the activist writer who died on the slopes of Mount Semeru in December 1969. The club climbs volcanoes, surveys forests and fosters a new love of the archipelago's wilderness among urban students.

Its members warn against the plunder of forests by the logging concessions now being granted to foreign and military-linked firms, and call for the protection of national parks and wildlife. Their influence is limited to campuses and the press, but their idealism links conservation to the student movement's demands for honest government.

18.name: Gerakan Mahasiswa Nasional Indonesia
18.text:
The Indonesian National Student Movement was founded in 1954 as the student organization of the nationalist movement around the PNI. Its left wing was purged after 1965, but it remains a large organization on campuses in Java and Bali, carrying the ideas of Sukarno's Marhaenism to a new generation.

GMNI calls for a socialist, independent Indonesia that protects small farmers and workers, limits foreign capital and stays non-aligned. It distrusts both the Islamic parties and the army's growing grip on politics. Its leverage lies in its network of student branches and in the enduring popularity of Sukarnoist ideas.

19.name: Partai Musyawarah Rakyat Banyak
19.text:
The Murba Party was founded in 1948 by followers of Tan Malaka, the independent communist executed in 1949 during the revolution. A bitter rival of the PKI, it was suspended by Sukarno in 1965 and rehabilitated by the New Order in 1966; its leading figures include Sukarni and Adam Malik, now Foreign Minister.

Murba advocates a national communism rooted in Indonesian conditions and independent of both Moscow and Beijing, with state control of key industries, land for peasants and an active non-aligned foreign policy. Its mass base is small, but its leaders' prominence in government gives it influence beyond its numbers.

20.name: Ikatan Pendukung Kemerdekaan Indonesia
20.english: League of Supporters of Indonesian Independence
20.text:
The League of Supporters of Indonesian Independence was founded in 1954 by army officers around Abdul Haris Nasution as a nationalist party loyal to the armed forces. Fiercely anti-communist, it supported the army throughout Guided Democracy and is preparing to contest the 1971 election.

IPKI preaches patriotic nationalism, the unity of the republic, the 1945 Constitution and a strong role for the military and veterans in national life. It rejects both communism and Islamic statehood. Its base is among veterans, officers' families and nationalist youth, and through its paramilitary offshoot it commands street muscle in North Sumatra.
20.wiki: League of Supporters of Indonesian Independence

21.name: Pemuda Pancasila
21.text:
Pancasila Youth was founded in 1959 as the youth wing of IPKI and became notorious in North Sumatra for its role in the killings of communists in 1965-66. Combining paramilitary drill with gangster networks around cinemas, markets and docks in Medan, it is protected by army officers who value its loyalty.

It preaches an aggressive nationalism of order, anti-communism and the sanctity of Pancasila, glorifying violence against the enemies of the nation. It has no coherent programme beyond loyalty to the regime and the spoils of protection rackets. Its leverage lies in its uniformed thousands, ready to intimidate opponents and mobilize crowds.

22.name: Angkatan Bersenjata Republik Indonesia
22.english: Armed Forces of the Republic of Indonesia
22.text:
The Armed Forces of the Republic of Indonesia, born in the revolution against the Dutch, have been the dominant power in the state since 1965. Suharto remains Minister of Defence and Security and supreme commander, with General Maraden Panggabean as his deputy, and officers hold ministries, governorships and posts throughout the bureaucracy.

Under the doctrine of dwifungsi, the military claims both a defence and a social-political role as guardian of the nation and Pancasila. It is fiercely anti-communist, cooperates with the United States and supports development under order. Its leverage is total: territorial commands reach every village, and no government can stand without it.

23.name: Kasultanan Ngayogyakarta Hadiningrat
23.text:
The Yogyakarta Sultanate, founded in 1755, is ruled by Sultan Hamengkubuwono IX, who sheltered the republic during the revolution and governs the Special Region of Yogyakarta. He also serves in Suharto's cabinet as Minister of State for Economic, Financial and Industrial Affairs, the most respected civilian in the New Order.

The sultanate stands for Javanese tradition, enlightened monarchy loyal to the republic and moderate, consensual government. It enjoys the reverence of Javanese across class lines, and the Sultan's reputation for integrity makes him a figure acceptable to students, Western donors and the army alike, a possible alternative leader.
